name: ConsensusRecSplit
workload: Construction of MPHFs over 100 million random string keys (length 10-50), comparing achieved bits/key against construction time versus RecSplit.
claimed_speedup: At 1.489 bits/key, ConsensusRecSplit constructs more than 350x faster than RecSplit, the previous state of the art at that space; given about an hour of construction time, it reaches 1.4448 bits/key (vs. a 1.4427 bit/key lower bound), where RecSplit only reaches 1.6127 bits/key in the same time.
hardware: Intel i7-11700, 2.5GHz base clock, 48KiB/512KiB L1/L2 per core, 16MiB L3
tradeoffs: Very slow in absolute terms at maximum space-efficiency settings (~1 hour for 100M keys); needs a large bucket size (e.g. k=32768) for the best trade-off; combines with a separate threshold-based k-perfect hash layer for cache locality, adding implementation complexity; GPL-3.0 + runtime exception licensing.
caveats: No direct BBHash/CMPH comparison is provided in the paper; the comparison is solely against RecSplit, the most directly comparable widely-used incumbent for this extreme space-efficiency regime.
found_via: GitHub: users/ByteHamster/repos listing

name: emphf
workload: Construction of MPHFs over 1 billion random 64-bit keys, comparing emphf against CMPH's CHD algorithm (mphf_benchmark table) and, separately, against the 'phf' library in rchikhi/benchmphf's own 1-billion-key test.
claimed_speedup: emphf builds in 374s at 2.61 bits/key versus CMPH's CHD needing 1972-23746s (5-63x slower) for 2.01-2.17 bits/key, per the mphf_benchmark reproduction on an Intel i9-9900K. Separately, rchikhi/benchmphf reports emphf's HEM variant building a 1-billion-key MPHF in 770s using 24GB RAM, versus the 'phf' library's 3900s and 48GB (about 5x faster, half the memory) -- that second comparison does not include CMPH numbers on the same page.
hardware: Intel i9-9900K @3.60GHz, 64GB DDR3 RAM @2.66GHz, Linux 5 (64-bit)
tradeoffs: Noticeably slower lookup (199 ns/key) than BBHash or PTHash in the same table; external-memory scan_mmap mode trades speed for lower construction memory; predates BBHash (2017) and PTHash (2021), so it was never tuned against them.
caveats: Project's own documentation only claims superiority over CMPH/MWHC-style peeling algorithms contemporary to its 2013-2014 publication, not over the newer fingerprinting/recursive-splitting families it is compared against here via a third-party benchmark.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "minimal perfect hash function" language:C++ --sort stars

name: PHast / PHast+ (bsuccinct-rs "ph" crate)
workload: MPHF construction (1 and 12 threads) and lookup on 5*10^7 and 5*10^8 uniformly random 64-bit integer keys; measures bits/key, query ns/key, and construction ns/key
claimed_speedup: At 5*10^7 keys: PHast (S=8, lambda=4.3, EF) reaches 1.94 bit/key, 10 ns/key query, 606 ns/key single-thread construction (69 ns/key at 12 threads), vs PTHash (lambda=5.0, EF) at 2.11 bit/key, 54 ns/key query, 577 ns/key construction (231 ns/key at 12 threads); PHast+ cuts single-thread construction to 61-140 ns/key (an order of magnitude faster than PHast) for 10-15 ns/key query (derived from page data, Table 5.2 of arXiv:2504.17918)
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.84.1 and gcc 12.2.0, both with third-level (-O3-equivalent) and CPU-native optimizations enabled
hardware: AMD Ryzen 5600G @ 3.9 GHz, 6 cores / 12 threads, 384KB/3MB/16MB L1/L2/L3 cache
tradeoffs: PHast/PHast+ trade small space overhead (~1.8-2.3 bits/key) for very simple, fast bucket-placement queries; PHast+ construction is 5-9x faster than PHast single-threaded and parallelizes near-linearly; PtrHash overtakes PHast on very large key sets once evaluation becomes memory-bandwidth bound. The same crate also ships FMPH/FMPHGO, fingerprinting-based MPHFs designed as a faster/smaller alternative to BBHash.
caveats: The Table 5.2/5.3 comparison is against other modern MPHFs (PTHash, PTHash-HEM, PHOBIC, PtrHash, SIMDRecSplit, SicHash, FMPH, FMPHGO), not directly against std::unordered_map, CMPH, or BBHash. The paper explicitly states it excluded BBHash from its own tests 'due to FMPH' already dominating it (citing Beling's 2023 ACM JEA paper, DOI 10.1145/3596453), so the FMPH-vs-BBHash numbers themselves were not independently re-verified on an accessible page this session.
found_via: gh search repos "minimal perfect hash" language:Rust --sort stars; cross-checked against PHast paper PDF (arXiv:2504.17918) Tables 5.2/5.3, read locally page-by-page after WebFetch's markdown conversion of the PDF failed

name: PTHash
workload: Construction and lookup of MPHFs over up to 1 billion pseudorandom 64-bit integer keys, 8-thread construction on one machine, reproducing Table 5 of the PTHash SIGIR'21 paper.
claimed_speedup: At similar space (~3 bits/key), PTHash looks up 3-4.6x faster than BBHash (37-55 ns/key for PTHash C-C/D-D variants vs 170 ns/key for BBHash gamma=1) on 1 billion 64-bit keys, though BBHash constructs faster (253s vs 689-1042s for PTHash) at that setting.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 9.2.1, -O3, -march=native (per PTHash SIGIR'21 paper methodology; same author/repo/hardware used for the reproduction table)
hardware: Intel i9-9900K @3.60GHz, 64GB DDR3 RAM @2.66GHz, Linux 5 (64-bit)
tradeoffs: Offline/batch construction only (not incremental); needs a 64-bit-bucket-id compile flag beyond 2^32 buckets; several encoder/bucketer configs (lambda, alpha, dense vs partitioned) must be tuned for the desired space/time trade-off.
caveats: Numbers come from a companion benchmark repo maintained by the same authors reproducing their own paper's table, not an independent third party. CMPH itself was not benchmarked directly: the PTHash authors state CMPH's FCH implementation was 'orders of magnitude slower' than their own faithful FCH reimplementation, so the CMPH comparison in the source table is via that reimplementation, not the CMPH library itself.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "minimal perfect hash function" language:C++ --sort stars

name: RecSplit (Sux C++ library)
workload: Construction and lookup of MPHFs over 1 billion random 64-bit keys, single machine, comparing RecSplit against CMPH's CHD algorithm (table reproducing Table 5 of the PTHash SIGIR'21 paper).
claimed_speedup: RecSplit (l=8, b=100) builds in 936s at 1.80 bits/key and 204 ns/key lookup, versus CMPH's CHD which needs 1972-23746s (2-25x slower) for a comparable-or-worse 2.01-2.17 bits/key; RecSplit is also far more compact than BBHash (1.80 vs 3.06-6.87 bits/key), though BBHash constructs faster.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 9.2.1, -O3, -march=native (mphf_benchmark harness, same environment as the PTHash paper)
hardware: Intel i9-9900K @3.60GHz, 64GB DDR3 RAM @2.66GHz, Linux 5 (64-bit)
tradeoffs: Recursive-splitting construction has higher constant factors than fingerprinting approaches (BBHash) at very low target space; single-header C++ template library requires manual integration; licensed GPL-3.0 + GCC Runtime Library Exception.
caveats: Numbers are sourced from a third-party benchmark repo (maintained by the PTHash authors) reproducing published results; vigna/sux's own README does not itself publish a CMPH comparison table, only pointers to the RecSplit paper and benchmark binaries.
found_via: GitHub: cross-referenced from ByteHamster/MPHF-Experiments README, which links RecSplit's canonical code location

name: ShockHash
workload: Construction of MPHFs for 10 million 64-bit keys at matched space (~1.56-1.59 bits/key), comparing RecSplit, SIMDRecSplit, and ShockHash-RS construction time per key (paper Table 1).
claimed_speedup: ShockHash-RS reaches 1.556 bits/key in 1,805 ns/key construction, about 75x faster than the next competitor at that space (SIMDRecSplit: 1.560 bits/key at 137,902 ns/key; plain RecSplit: 1.585 bits/key at 125,521 ns/key).
hardware: Intel i7-11700, 8 cores, 2.5GHz base, Ubuntu 22.04
tradeoffs: Base case is exponential-time in theory (mitigated by integrating into RecSplit-style partitioning); space-optimal configurations still take much longer to build than fingerprinting methods in absolute terms; SIMD variants need AVX support; GPL-3.0 + runtime exception licensing.
caveats: The paper explicitly states BBHash was left out of these plots because it is 'significantly outperformed by FMPH' (a Rust library), and CMPH is not compared at all, so there is no direct BBHash/CMPH number here; baseline is recorded honestly as RecSplit, the closest widely-used incumbent actually tested, with baseline_in_list=false.
found_via: GitHub: users/ByteHamster/repos listing, cross-referenced via ByteHamster/MPHF-Experiments README

name: SimdRecSplit / GpuRecSplit
workload: Construction of MPHFs for 10 million 64-bit keys on one 8-core CPU (SimdRecSplit) or a GPU (GpuRecSplit), comparing bits/key and construction ns/key against RecSplit and BBHash (paper Table 3).
claimed_speedup: SIMDRecSplit reaches 2.96 bits/key at 49 ns/key construction, beating BBHash's gamma=1.0 setting (3.059 bits/key at 208 ns/key) on both space and speed (about 4x faster) for 10M keys; the GPU version (GpuRecSplit) adds up to a 5438x speedup over the original single-threaded RecSplit implementation.
hardware: Intel i7-11700 (8 cores/16 threads, 2.5GHz base, AVX-512); NVIDIA RTX 3090 for the GPU variant
tradeoffs: GPU variant requires CUDA hardware/drivers; SIMD variant needs AVX support (falls back to slower emulated SIMD without it); licensed GPL-3.0 + GCC Runtime Library Exception (same terms as libstdc++), which is more restrictive than BBHash's/PTHash's permissive licenses.
caveats: The BBHash comparison numbers were extracted from the arXiv HTML rendering of the paper via an automated fetch/summarize step, not manually cross-checked line-by-line against the PDF; the README's own headline table only compares against RecSplit/SIMDRecSplit, not BBHash, across its full parameter sweep.
found_via: GitHub: ByteHamster org repo listing (users/ByteHamster/repos), cross-referenced via ByteHamster/MPHF-Experiments README

name: LPHash
workload: Building a locality-preserving MPHF over sets of overlapping k-mers (k=31/47/63) extracted from stitched genomic unitigs.
claimed_speedup: README states LPHash achieves under 0.9 bits/k-mer in practice, versus a 1.44 bits/k-mer theoretical MPHF lower bound and 2-3 bits/k-mer for practical general-purpose MPHF constructions.
tradeoffs: Specialized for consecutive/overlapping k-mer key sets in bioinformatics, not a general-purpose MPHF; requires k-mer-specific preprocessing (stitched unitig files); partitioned vs. unpartitioned construction is a further trade-off between memory and speed.
caveats: The specific competitor behind the '2-3 bits/k-mer' figure is not named on the page (only 'practical constructions'), so the baseline here is a best guess and confidence is capped accordingly, per the hard rule on unnamed baselines. Published in a peer-reviewed venue (Bioinformatics/ISMB), giving Tier B despite the unconfirmed hardware/compiler.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "minimal perfect hash" --sort stars

name: MorphisHash
workload: Space overhead of the constructed MPHF's seed/candidate-position encoding, compared to ShockHash's two-candidate-position redundancy, on the same key-set construction workload used in ShockHash's own experiments
claimed_speedup: Saves Theta(ln n) bits versus ShockHash; corresponds to a factor of about 20x less space overhead in practice (verbatim from the MorphisHash paper abstract, arXiv:2503.10161)
tradeoffs: GitHub fork of ByteHamster/ShockHash that changes the seed-encoding scheme to remove redundant key-to-position mappings, reducing space at the same query complexity; integrated as its own contender in ByteHamster/MPHF-Experiments; very low external adoption (3 stars) despite the algorithmic improvement
caveats: Only the paper abstract was accessible this session (PDF/HTML full-text fetch failed for ar5iv/arxiv.org/html), so exact bits/key and ns/key figures from the paper's results tables were not directly confirmed; the '20x less space overhead' figure applies only to the redundancy component of ShockHash's space, not to total bits/key. Baseline (ShockHash) is itself an advanced research MPHF, not std::unordered_map/CMPH/BBHash.
found_via: gh api repos/ByteHamster/MPHF-Experiments/readme, which links MorphisHash's code at stefanfred/MorphisHash and cites arXiv:2503.10161

name: PHOBIC-GPU
workload: GPU-accelerated construction of a minimal perfect hash function at a configuration tuned for fast queries, vs the CPU PHOBIC construction algorithm
claimed_speedup: PHOBIC-GPU constructs an MPHF at 2.17 bits/key in 28 ns/key on GPU (Vulkan), queryable in 37 ns on the CPU (verbatim from the PHOBIC paper abstract, arXiv:2404.18497)
tradeoffs: Requires Vulkan-capable GPU for construction; only construction is GPU-accelerated, queries still run on CPU; the CPU PHOBIC implementation it accelerates lives inside the already-catalogued jermp/pthash repo (branch 'phobic'), so this repo only supplies the GPU construction path
caveats: Full paper text (PDF/HTML) could not be retrieved this session (conversion errors on ar5iv and arxiv.org/html), so only the abstract's numbers were confirmed; exact GPU model, CPU-vs-GPU speedup ratio, and compiler flags are unconfirmed. Only 4 GitHub stars. Benchmarked against the paper's own PHOBIC-CPU baseline, not std::unordered_map, CMPH, or BBHash.
found_via: ByteHamster/MPHF-Experiments README (gh api repos/ByteHamster/MPHF-Experiments/readme), which lists PHOBIC-GPU as a benchmarked contender with a link to stefanfred/PHOBIC-GPU; corroborated by WebSearch "PHOBIC perfect hashing github ByteHamster"

name: PtrHash
workload: MPHF construction and lookup on up to 1 billion random 64-bit integer keys and on 300 million string keys; measures bits/key, query ns/key (loop and streaming/prefetched), and construction ns/key
claimed_speedup: At least 2.1x faster queries than PTHash/PHOBIC on 300M string keys; 3.3x speedup with streaming queries; 12 ns/key query in a for-loop (down to 8 ns/key streaming) on 1B integer keys at 2.0-3.0 bits/key
hardware: Intel Core i7-10750H, 6 cores, hyper-threading disabled, frequency pinned to 2.6 GHz
tradeoffs: Rust implementation; an unofficial, ambiguously-licensed C++ port exists (bassiounix/PtrHash-cc, made for an LLVM libc RFC) but has no independent benchmarks; CompactPtrHash trades ~2x slower construction for smaller size; needs sharding for keys that don't fit in RAM
caveats: Paper (SEA 2025) benchmarks against PTHash, PHOBIC, SIMDRecSplit and Consensus-RecSplit, not directly against std::unordered_map, CMPH, or BBHash; text explicitly says BBHash/CMPH-style fingerprinting methods are not competitive and are omitted. Compiler/flags for the main experiments are not stated in the paper (only that the implementation is Rust), so evidence is capped below Tier A.
found_via: arXiv API query all:"minimal perfect hash" AND all:"construction" sorted by submission date; PtrHash paper arXiv:2502.15539, cross-checked via gh search repos "ptrhash"

name: SicHash
workload: Construction-time/query-time/space Pareto comparison for (minimal) perfect hash functions over large key sets, plotted against competing PHFs including BBHash- and CMPH-style approaches (ALENEX'23 paper, linked plots).
claimed_speedup: README states SicHash 'offers a very good trade-off between construction performance, query performance, and space consumption' relative to prior work, shown via Pareto plots linked from the README and hosted on arXiv; exact numeric ratios against BBHash/CMPH could not be extracted from the paper text this session.
tradeoffs: Depends on the BuRR retrieval data structure as a submodule; cuckoo-hashing-based construction with overloading needs careful parameter tuning; plain GPLv3 licensing (no stated runtime exception).
caveats: Could not independently verify the exact CPU/compiler details or extract the BBHash/CMPH numeric comparison from the paper's PDF/HTML this session (extraction attempts returned only partial/garbled text), so the numbers referenced are qualitative (from the README) rather than quoted figures, capping evidence at Tier C with reduced confidence.
found_via: GitHub: users/ByteHamster/repos listing

name: fastcpp::phf (developer source)
workload: 200k keyword lookups against a 92-key C++20 keyword table (fastcpp::phf, a compiler-built perfect hash baked into .rodata) compared to std::unordered_map<string_view,uint16_t>, measured separately for all-hit, all-miss, and 1:8-mixed-hit-rate corpora.
claimed_speedup: 6.98x on all-hit lookups (3.327ns vs 23.208ns/op), 6.70x on all-miss (3.02ns vs 20.243ns), 5.76x on mixed 1:8 (4.903ns vs 28.235ns) -- verbatim from results/fastest.json. Also beats phmap::flat_hash_map (Apache-2.0, vendored in-repo) 3.7x and frozen::unordered_map 3.5-3.7x on the same static workload, though the frozen comparison is weaker evidence (see caveats).
hardware: Intel Xeon @ 2.10GHz (AVX2, SSE4.2, BMI2), 4 cores, Ubuntu 24.04 / Linux 6.18 -- a shared cloud VM; the repo's own results file warns absolute ns move between runs on this host (ratios within a run are what is claimed as stable)
tradeoffs: Only usable when the key set is closed at compile time (keywords, opcodes, enum labels) -- no runtime insert/delete. The shipped default comparison policy (std::memcmp) is not the fastest one measured: compare_policy::overread16 is 1.44x faster still but requires 16 readable bytes at the query pointer, so it is opt-in rather than default. Table size scales with key count and is baked into .rodata, growing binary size. Requires a C++20-capable compiler (gcc 13+/clang 17+/MSVC 19.35+) for the constexpr search; clang needs a much larger constexpr-step budget than gcc for the same search.
caveats: Repo is PRIVATE, readable only via the authenticated gh CLI (gh api repos/private:developer-source/...); 0 GitHub stars; appears to be a single-author, AI-assisted project (commits authored/co-authored by 'Claude', SSH-signature verified) with no external review. The std::unordered_map comparison above is Tier A: bench/bench_phf.cpp is public in the repo and compiler, flags, and CPU model are all stated for the run that produced the numbers. The frozen::unordered_map comparison (3.5-3.7x) cited in results/fastest.json and third_party/parallel-hashmap/VENDORING.md is weaker: the current bench/bench_vs_libraries.cpp (checked at HEAD and at the commit that recorded the number, 2e21aae) only benchmarks fastcpp::phf, phmap::flat_hash_map, and std::unordered_map in code -- frozen is referenced only in comments as a claim from a benchmark that was run during evaluation but whose code was not committed, so that specific figure is first-party/Tier C, not independently reproducible from the tree as it stands today. No gperf comparison exists anywhere in the repo (README or results), despite gperf being in this project's baseline list.
found_via: seed-record pass: gh api repos/private:developer-source/contents/results/fastest.json, cross-checked against bench/bench_phf.cpp, bench/bench_vs_libraries.cpp, include/fastcpp/phf/, third_party/parallel-hashmap/VENDORING.md, and the repo README

name: fph-table (Flash Perfect Hash)
workload: Lookup (successful 'find') of 64-bit integer keys at 0.9 max_load_factor across table sizes from 32 to 10^7, run by the independent hashtable-bench suite across std::unordered_map, ska::flat_hash_map, absl::flat_hash_map, tsl::robin_map, emhash7, robin_hood, and fph::DynamicFphMap/MetaFphMap
claimed_speedup: fph::DynamicFphMap (with fph::SimpleSeedHash) has the fastest lookup once the table exceeds ~1,000 elements on x86-64 (AMD 3990X) and the fastest lookup at every tested size on arm64 (Apple M1 Max), ahead of std::unordered_map and every other tested map in the hashtable-bench charts; a second independent suite (Martin Ankerl's 2022 hashmap benchmark, Intel i7-8700 @3200MHz, clang++13 -O3 -march=native) separately reports fph::DynamicFphMap find as 'extremely fast, regardless of the hash'
compiler_and_flags: gcc 10.2.0 -O3 (AMD 3990X, Ubuntu 20.04, CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release); clang 13.1.6 (Apple M1 Max, macOS 12.1); separately clang++13 -O3 -march=native on the Ankerl benchmark
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper 3990X (Zen2); Apple M1 Max; Intel Xeon E-2388G (Rocket Lake, per the hashtable-bench blog); Intel i7-8700 @3200MHz (Ankerl benchmark)
tradeoffs: Dynamic perfect hash table rebuilds the whole table whenever an insert breaks perfectness, so insert/erase are slow and are 'the slowest in the benchmark' per the Ankerl suite; needs a seed-aware hash functor (not plain std::hash) unless using the no-seed branch; keys must be CopyConstructible, values MoveConstructible; MetaFphMap trades hit-lookup speed for faster miss-lookup
caveats: Exact ns/op figures live in PNG charts in hashtable-bench and in a normalized (base-100) interactive table on Ankerl's blog, not as machine-readable numbers pulled into this record; hashtable-bench is maintained by the same author as fph-table (though it independently tests many third-party maps), while the Ankerl suite is fully independent
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "CHD algorithm hash" / "fast lookup table generator" -> renzibei/fph-table
gh search repos "perfect hash" --sort stars; WebSearch "perfect hash C++ library faster than unordered_map github 2025 2026"

name: frozen
baseline: std::set, std::unordered_set (same constexpr perfect-hash design also backs frozen::unordered_map, the drop-in for std::unordered_map)
workload: Single-lookup microbenchmark of present/absent int and string keys in small (~dozens of keys) frozen containers vs. the equivalent std:: container.
claimed_speedup: frozen::unordered_set ~3.1x faster than std::unordered_set for present int keys (173 ns vs 544 ns), ~3.8x for absent keys (131 ns vs 500 ns); frozen::set ~2.6x faster than std::set for present int keys (58 ns vs 153 ns); string containers ~1.7x (set) to ~3.3x (unordered_set, absent key) faster (derived from page data)
hardware: Intel Core i7-6600U CPU @ 2.60GHz
tradeoffs: Containers are immutable/fixed-capacity: no insert/erase/rehash after construction (constexpr keys are permanently fixed; without constexpr, values may be updated but keys cannot). Compile time and template-instantiation cost grow with key-set size. Header-only, no runtime dependency.
caveats: Numbers are from a February 2018 Quarkslab blog post written by the library's own author, not from a benchmark artifact committed in the repo (the repo ships the bench source under benchmarks/ but no published results file). The cited numbers are for frozen::set/unordered_set vs std::set/std::unordered_set, not literally std::unordered_map, though frozen::unordered_map uses the same perfect-hash mechanism. Which standard-library implementation (libstdc++ vs libc++) Clang++-5.0 linked against is not stated. A second, earlier (2017) Quarkslab post comparing frozen to gperf and std::unordered_set on a dictionary-lookup task did not state compiler/hardware and measured wall-clock time that the author flagged as likely I/O-bound, so that post was not used as the primary source.
found_via: WebSearch: "frozen c++ header-only constexpr unordered_map benchmark speedup vs std::unordered_map" -> https://blog.quarkslab.com/frozen-zero-cost-initialization-for-immutable-containers-and-various-algorithms.html; repo found via gh search repos "gperf" language:C++

name: hashify
workload: Median per-lookup time (criterion) on real key sets (HTTP methods, IMAP commands, Sieve keywords, charset names, HTML entities) and synthetic 10k/100k random string keys, for sequential 'hits' and pseudo-random 'random' lookup patterns
claimed_speedup: hashify's map! macro is 4.1x-12.6x faster than the phf crate's default CHD layout and 3.2x-8.8x faster than phf's experimental ptrhash layout across all tested key sets; also faster than a plain Rust match for larger key sets (e.g. 25.1-39.8ns for match vs 1.85-1.95ns for hashify on the 2125-entry HTML-entity table)
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.98, criterion default release settings (opt-level=3 noted separately for the build-time table)
hardware: Apple M5 Max
tradeoffs: Rust-only procedural macro; tables are built at proc-macro expansion time so a large key set adds real build time (up to ~24s for 1,000,000 keys, worse without opt-level=3); cannot rebuild tables at runtime; not usable from C++
caveats: Benchmark is first-party (project's own README/criterion suite), but hardware, Rust version, and exact bench commands are all stated and reproducible (cargo bench --bench lookup), satisfying Tier A; no independent third-party confirmation found this session
found_via: gh search repos "perfect hash" --sort stars

name: phashtable (gsauthof)
workload: Repeated random-slot lookup micro-benchmark (probing all slots of a table built from real-world ISIN identifier strings, 2,776 to 1.4M items) comparing a 2-level perfect hash table against std::unordered_map, each combined with 3 hash functions (sdbm, SipHash, and a stock/library default), with min/max per-lookup latency measured on an isolated, frequency-locked core
claimed_speedup: On an Intel Atom C3758: ptable_sdbm latency is 43-44ns (1ns min-max spread) vs umap_sdbm 22-61ns (39ns spread); on an Intel Xeon Gold 6246: ptable_sdbm 11-12ns vs umap_sdbm 9-34ns (25ns spread). The perfect hash table is not faster in minimum-case latency (umap_sdbm's minimum is actually lower on both CPUs), but its worst-case latency and jitter are far more consistent than std::unordered_map's, whose access time varies up to ~3x due to collision resolution
compiler_and_flags: g++ -std=gnu++17 -Wall -O3 -march=goldmont-plus (Atom C3758 build); GCC 9 (Xeon Gold 6246, RHEL 7)
hardware: Intel Atom C3758 (Fedora 31, process pinned to an isolated core, frequency management disabled); Intel Xeon Gold 6246 (RHEL 7, isolated core, frequency locked to 4.1GHz)
tradeoffs: Static/rebuild-only table (no incremental insert/delete, meant to be built at startup or re-init); ~8.6 bytes/item overhead vs ~5.33 bytes/item for a 75%-loaded open-addressing hash table; gperf comparison in its own docs notes gperf doesn't terminate in reasonable time on the same 1.4M-key ISIN set
caveats: The project's actual claim is about latency *jitter*/worst-case consistency, not raw average speed: std::unordered_map's best-case latency is lower than the perfect hash table's on both tested CPUs, so 'faster' only clearly holds for tail latency and consistency, not the mean/min case; benchmark hardware and compiler flags for the C++ side are fully stated (build-bench.sh), so despite the nuance this is graded Tier A on methodology
found_via: WebSearch "perfect hash C++ library faster than unordered_map github 2025 2026"

name: static_maps
workload: Construction + lookup runtime on three demos run 10,000+ times each: (1) average isotopic mass lookup by element symbol (1024 random lookups per run), (2) amino-acid-from-codon translation (65,536 codons per run), (3) in-place random modification of S&P 500 stock prices by ticker symbol
claimed_speedup: static_maps::unordered_map runtime is <40% of std::unordered_map on the elements demo (35.8 vs 89.6 microsec avg), <35% on the codon demo (607.6 vs 1746.8 microsec avg), and <73% on the stocks demo (~15295 vs ~21228 microsec avg); also <80%/<45%/<97% of frozen::unordered_map on the same three demos, <35% of a PTHash-based lookup, and <89% of a gperf-generated map (single demo tested for PTHash/gperf)
compiler_and_flags: g++ 15.2.1, -std=c++23 -O3 -march=native (plus -fconstexpr-ops-limit=100000000 to 20000000000 to allow compile-time construction of the larger tables; also verified to compile under clang 21.1.6 with -fconstexpr-steps raised)
hardware: Intel Core i5-1240P @4.4GHz laptop CPU, 12 cores/24 threads, 448KiB/640KiB L1, 9MiB L2, 12MiB L3 cache; nice -20, chrt -f 98 real-time priority, ASLR disabled
tradeoffs: consteval/constexpr-only: the full keyset must be known at compile time; compile time is much higher than std (e.g. 55.2s vs 1.5s for the stock demo) and requires raising the compiler's constexpr step/ops limits, sometimes to values that risk long or failing builds on large keysets; drop-in only for std::unordered_map's operator[]/at() access pattern, not the full container API (e.g. custom KeyEqual/Allocator need modification)
caveats: Code is distributed as a Figshare software deposit (DOI), not a live GitHub repo, so there is no commit history or star count to check ongoing maintenance; the figshare landing page returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch this session, so availability was confirmed only via the DOI redirect and the paper's own citation of the deposit, not by directly viewing the hosted files

name: cmph / cxxmph (mph_map)
workload: Lookup-heavy workload over large sets of URL keys (>100k) comparing cxxmph's mph_map/mph_set (BDZ-algorithm minimal perfect hash wrapped in an unordered_map-compatible interface) against std::unordered_map.
claimed_speedup: "about 10%-50% faster than unordered_map" for large (>100k) URL key sets with expensive comparisons (verbatim from the header comment)
tradeoffs: cxxmph containers are read-mostly: cheap lookups but the perfect hash is rebuilt on structural change, so it favors static/rarely-modified key sets. Author's own comment warns "those classes are not necessarily faster than their existing counterparts, benchmark your code before using it." Core cmph library targets very large (up to billions of) key sets, unlike gperf which targets small compile-time sets.
caveats: The 10-50% figure has no stated methodology at all (no benchmark code, compiler, flags, hardware, or dataset size beyond ">100k"), capping it at C. The GitHub mirror's last commit is from 2017 and the repo is effectively unmaintained; the underlying cmph project's canonical home is a SourceForge/Google Code-era release, so provenance of this mirror is secondary rather than primary.

name: constexpr-phf (Kronuz/phf)
baseline: std::unordered_map, std::set, if-ladder, switch (binary search), gperf
workload: Integer-core find() at N=6..1000 keys; string dispatch benchmark hashing Xapiand's 192 field-type names, and a 570-word English stop-word filter over a 464K-word text, comparing hash-only and hash+verify constexpr-phf lookup against gperf, frozen::unordered_set, a compile-time trie, std::unordered_map and std::set.
claimed_speedup: vs unordered_map/if-ladder/switch: 1.2-1.3 ns/lookup for phf at N=6..1000 vs 2.4-162 ns (if-ladder), 4.0-40 ns (switch), 3.1-3.2 ns (unordered_map). String dispatch (192 field-type names): gperf 14 ns, phf hash-only 18 ns, phf hash+verify 21 ns, compile-time trie 28 ns, std::unordered_map 29 ns, frozen::unordered_set 40 ns, std::set 82 ns/op
hardware: x86_64 (no specific CPU model stated)
tradeoffs: Integer keys only (strings must be pre-hashed by the caller, and hash-only lookups can misdispatch a non-member key unless verified). Fixed key set at build time, no insert/erase/rehash. Large key sets increase compile time since the perfect hash is searched at compile time.
caveats: First-party benchmark (project's own README/bench code); capped at C because hardware is stated only as "x86_64" with no CPU model, even though compiler and flags (GCC 11, -O3) are given. Numbers for gperf/frozen/trie come from the same repo's bench/ harness, not independently reproduced.

name: ConstexprCore/perfect_hash
baseline: std::unordered_map, gperf, frozen::unordered_map, absl::flat_hash_map, pthash, ankerl::unordered_dense, if/else chain
workload: Billion-queries-per-second table for the URL-protocol key set (http, https, ftp, ws, wss, file); a broader benchmark suite also covers S&P 100 tickers, C++ keywords, HTTP headers, MIME types, letters a-z, and JS reserved words, each queried hit-only/miss-only/mixed.
claimed_speedup: 1.08 billion queries/s for this library vs 0.23 (gperf), 0.22 (kronuz::phf), 0.16 (frozen::unordered_map), 0.14 (absl::flat_hash_map / pthash), 0.10 (std::unordered_map / ankerl::dense_hash_map), 0.19 (naive) -- roughly 10x std::unordered_map and 4x the next-fastest competitor
hardware: Apple M4
tradeoffs: Wide container needed past 255 keys or 254-byte keys (different code path, whole-key multiplicative hash). Requires C++23. Compile time grows with key-set size (raising -fconstexpr-steps/-fconstexpr-ops-limit is needed for large sets, e.g. ~5s for 5,581 keys).
caveats: No compiler name or optimization flags are stated for the headline billion-queries/s table (only "Apple M4 processor"), so it is capped at C despite the CPU model being named. The claimed 10x-over-unordered_map and 4x-over-next-competitor gap is large for a 6-key set; new project (first commit era unclear, 17 stars) so treat as an unverified first-party claim pending independent reproduction.

name: icy
workload: map/set find() and iteration for std::string_view and std::int64_t keys at N=16/512/1024, comparing icy::map/set (consteval-built, open-addressed) against std::map, std::unordered_map/set, tsl::robin_map/set, and a sorted-vector binary search.
claimed_speedup: std::string_view find() at N=1024: icy 3.228 cycles/op vs std::map 44.393, std::unordered_map 5.278, tsl::robin_map 4.595, sorted-vector+lb 23.987 (roughly 1.5-2x faster than std::unordered_map/set per the README's own summary, and up to ~14x faster than std::map, derived from page data)
hardware: Apple M4 Max
tradeoffs: Best for small key sets; larger sets (>=1000) need -fconstexpr-steps tuning. Requires C++23 and consteval support. An ICY_OPTIMIZE_KEY_CMP macro skips key comparison in find() for extra speed at the cost of relying purely on hash equality.
caveats: Build config for the benchmark is RelWithDebInfo (not a bare -O3 Release build) and no compiler name/version or exact flags are given, so this is capped at C despite the CPU model being named. Brand-new project (0 stars, first commits recent), numbers are the author's own microbenchmark, not independently reproduced.

name: mph (qlibs)
workload: Lookup of small compile-time-known string/int static maps (5-149 entries: random strings of length 4, 8, mixed 1-8, and random uint keys) run with the qlibs/mph benchmark harness against std::map, std::unordered_map, boost::unordered_map, boost::flat_map, and gperf-generated C code
claimed_speedup: mph is fastest in every row under both g++ and clang++: e.g. random_strings_5_len_4 - std::unordered_map 5.56ns vs mph 1.61ns (~3.5x); random_strings_100_len_8 - std::unordered_map 15.32ns vs mph 1.58ns (~9.7x), gperf 8.04ns vs mph 1.58ns (~5.1x)
tradeoffs: Requires C++20 (gcc-12+/clang-15+); keys/values must be fully known at compile time (constexpr array), not a general dynamic hash table; author states it targets thousands, not millions, of entries; optional bmi2/SIMD hardware acceleration
caveats: First-party benchmark; compiler and flags are stated but no CPU model is given, so this is capped at Tier C per the rules (partial methodology) even though the numbers themselves look plausible (3-10x, not an outlier ratio) and are not independently reproduced

name: Perfect::Hash / pperf
workload: Lookup time over a 99,171-key dictionary (linux/amd64) and a medium 2,000-key dictionary, comparing generated perfect-hash C code (hanovpp/hanov/urban/pearson/cmph-* variants) and a generated switch table against gperf-generated C code
claimed_speedup: On the 99,171-key dictionary gperf fails to complete ('-1 errors... killed') while hanovpp/hanov/urban finish and achieve 0.007-0.014s total lookup time; on the 2,000-key dictionary gperf itself has the fastest lookup (0.001428s) but the slowest compile time (0.87s vs 0.08-0.14s for the Perl::Hash algorithms)
hardware: Intel Core i5-2300 CPU @ 2.80GHz
tradeoffs: The Perl module is a CPAN generator; it produces plain C output that is directly usable from C/C++. Result is nuanced: gperf actually wins on raw lookup latency for small dictionaries and only fails to scale (times out/dies) on very large ones; a plain generated switch table has an impractical 36+ second compile time and a huge generated source file. Repo is self-described as 'alpha'
caveats: Own benchmark script (examples/bench.pl); CPU model is stated but the compiler/flags used to build the generated C benchmark harness are not shown in the README, so this is capped at Tier C; treat the 'beats gperf' framing narrowly as a scalability win, not a universal speed win
found_via: gh search repos "topic:perfect-hash" --sort stars

name: strager/perfect-hash-tables
workload: Google Benchmark loop looking up identifier tokens (lexed from three quick-lint-js-style corpora: keywords-only, non-keywords-only, and a mixed file, each ~287KB of source) against dozens of generated perfect-hash-table (pht), gperf, mygperf, frozen::unordered_map, and std::unordered_map implementations compiled as shared libraries and dlopen'd by benchmark.cpp.
claimed_speedup: notes.txt (author's dev log): nonkeywords workload - icrc32 hasher w/ --string-compare=check1memcmp pht (~69 us) outperforms gperf default (~95 us) [~1.4x, derived from page data]; mixed workload - same pht config (~152 us) outperforms gperf default (~188 us) [~1.24x, derived from page data]. Same notes also record frozen::unordered_map+lehmer128 as slower than this pht config in both workloads (~85 us and ~209 us respectively). On the keywords-only workload the note states gperf beats all of the author's own hashing algorithms with --string-compare=memcmp, and is only 'competitive' with icrc32 when gperf uses --string-compare=check1memcmp - i.e. pht does NOT win that workload.
compiler_and_flags: Makefile: Linux uses g++-12 (and a stage-2 Clang build) with -std=c++20 -g -O3 -fvisibility=hidden -fPIC -fcf-protection=full -msse4 -maes; macOS (arm64) uses Apple Clang with Homebrew google-benchmark 1.7.1, same -std=c++20 -O3 -fPIC baseline flags (SSE/AES flags are Linux-only).
hardware: notes.txt states 'my 5950X' (AMD Ryzen 9 5950X) for the `perf stat` branch-prediction measurements earlier in the same file; the wall-clock microsecond figures quoted for the gperf-vs-pht comparison appear in the same notes.txt session but the CPU is not re-stated next to those specific numbers, so the hardware attribution is inferred from proximity, not restated per-benchmark.
tradeoffs: Perfect-hash tables require the full keyword/key set to be known at build time (code-generation step via generate-pht.cpp / generate-mygperf.py / gperf itself), so they are not usable as a general-purpose associative container; no insertion/deletion at runtime; many generated variants trade code size and branch-predictability for speed (e.g. AES-hasher variants generate much larger .cpp files than FNV/lehmer128 ones); results are highly sensitive to table-size, hasher choice (icrc32/fnv1a32/lehmer128/pearson8/aes/xx364), string-compare strategy (memcmp/check1memcmp/chunk84/cmpestri/sse2/ptest), and CPU features (msse4/maes/cmov), meaning the 'winning' configuration is workload- and hardware-specific rather than a single drop-in replacement.
caveats: Capped at Tier C rather than A: the concrete '~69 us / ~95 us' style numbers in notes.txt are the author's own rounded dev-log figures with methodology and hardware only loosely (not explicitly per-number) restated, per the rule that a project's own benchmark code with partial methodology is C, not B/A. The repo contains no committed results file or CI benchmark log with exact reproducible output for these numbers - only the source (benchmark.cpp, Makefile, generated/ implementations) and the free-text notes.txt. The comparison is workload-dependent and partly cherry-picked: pht only beats gperf on the nonkeywords and mixed corpora, and explicitly loses to gperf on the keywords-only corpus. LICENSE is CC-BY-NC-ND-4.0 (confirmed by decoding the LICENSE file via the GitHub contents API) - non-OSI, 'EDUCATIONAL USE ONLY' per README.md, so usability is 'reference' (study only, do not copy the code; also carries no patent grant). Repo has had no commits since 2023-03-12 (>3 years) and is unarchived but functionally abandoned. The companion talk (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DMQ_HcNSOAI, title 'Faster than Rust and C++: the PERFECT hash table') could not be fetched this session (YouTube pages are not readable by the available tools), so its stated final speedup numbers are NOT reflected here - this record relies solely on the repo's own benchmark code and notes.txt. The technique here has been independently reimplemented from scratch in private:developer-source (fastcpp::phf); that is a separate, newer implementation, not evidence for this repo's own numbers.

name: triehash
workload: Hash 1,000,000 times per word over the field names of Debian Packages/Sources files, measured in GB/s, across 7 machines/architectures (amd64, arm64, armel, armhf, ppc64el, mipsel).
claimed_speedup: On jak-x230 (amd64, Core i5-3320M): order-preserving Trie 2.4 GB/s vs gperf 1.3 GB/s (case-sensitive) / 0.7 GB/s (case-insensitive, "gperf (*)") -- roughly 1.8-3.4x faster than gperf depending on variant and architecture (derived from page data)
hardware: Mixed: "jak-x230" (stated elsewhere as Core i5-3320M), plus unnamed Debian porterbox machines for the other architectures
stars_or_usage: 49 stars; used in APT (Debian package manager)
tradeoffs: Order-preserving (unlike most minimal perfect hash schemes), which trades some construction flexibility for keeping key order in the output table. Generator only handles a fixed key set known at generation time (codegen tool, like gperf, not a runtime container).
caveats: Compiler (and its version/flags) is not stated for any of the measured machines, only listed as gcc-family via context; most machines beyond the x230 are named only by hostname, not CPU model, so hardware is only partially identified. It's a C code generator, not a C++ template library, but is directly callable from C++ (per the assignment's C-API rule).
